conventions.convention: Sufficiency uses standard Borel data and statistic spaces and one everywhere probability kernel independent of the parameter; its conditional identities hold under every model law.
Completeness tests measurable real functions integrable under every parameter; zero expectation under every law implies almost-sure vanishing separately under every law.
Minimal sufficiency compares with every sufficient sub-sigma-field, modulo measurable sets null under every model law; statistic minimality means minimality of its generated sigma-field.
Ancillarity means the entire pushforward law is parameter-independent.
Full rank requires an open natural-parameter subset and absence of a nontrivial affine constraint on T almost everywhere on {h>0}; the base measure is sigma-finite and normalization is log Z.
The common-reference equivalence requires a dominating reference law belonging to the model; derivative exceptional sets may depend on the parameter.

Discrete likelihood-ratio equivalence is defined on a common support where every point has strictly positive probability under every parameter; the quotient has the discrete sigma-field and off-support assignments are common-null.
The likelihood-ratio vector uses a countable family indexed k≥1, strictly positive mixture weights, and finite nonnegative density versions reset on one common Q-null set.
Transform uniqueness assumes AC, finite total variation, an exponential moment, and vanishing on a real neighborhood of zero; dimension zero is included.

load_bearing.statement: T is sufficient if there is one probability kernel K from the standard Borel statistic space to the standard Borel data space such that Pθ(A∩T⁻¹(C))=∫C K(y,A) Pθᵀ(dy) for every θ, A, and C.

For standard Borel data and statistic spaces, a nonempty model, an in-model reference P0, and Pθ≪P0 for every θ, T is sufficient if and only if every derivative dPθ/dP0 has a σ(T)-measurable version, equivalently a finite nonnegative Borel factor gθ(T). Exceptional null sets may depend on θ.

A sufficient sigma-field G* is minimal sufficient if G*⊆H modulo the family-null ideal for every sufficient H. Sufficiency requires common bounded conditional-expectation versions for every bounded measurable real u.
For every measurable real g integrable under every parameter, Eθ[g(T)]=0 for every θ implies Pθ(g(T)=0)=1 for every θ.
Assume AC and k≥0. A finite complex Borel measure ν on Rᵏ with ∫exp(δ‖x‖₁)|ν|(dx)<∞ for some δ>0 is zero if its Laplace transform vanishes on a real open neighborhood of zero.

Assume AC. Every nonempty family of probability measures dominated by a sigma-finite positive measure admits a finite or countable positive-weight mixture of its members that dominates every family member.
Assume AC. A full-rank exponential family as defined here, whose natural parameter set contains a nonempty open subset of Rᵏ, has complete canonical statistic T.
On a standard Borel sample space, if standard Borel statistics T and U are respectively complete sufficient and ancillary, then T and U are independent under every model law.

Assume AC. For a countable family on a standard Borel space and a strictly positive-weight mixture Q, the vector of finite Borel densities dPk/dQ, reset on one common Q-null set, is minimal sufficient. It factors Q-almost surely through every standard Borel sufficient statistic.

Assume AC. Under the common positive discrete-support hypotheses, the likelihood-ratio equivalence-class statistic, with any fixed class assigned off the support, is minimal sufficient modulo the support complement.

concerns.concern: The Statement and Given omit AC, although A1 says 'the Radon–Nikodym theorem is used under AC' and proof steps use AC-qualified RN existence, standard-Borel coding, and conditional-distribution existence. The proof is sound under that explicitly supplied assumption; the public Statement should carry the same choice qualification.

Under 'Statement refuted', the item states 'A curved exponential subfamily can have a sufficient canonical statistic that is not complete.' This is the true existence claim proved by the example, rather than the false completeness assertion being refuted. The witness and its expectation calculation are sound; the heading or formulation should identify the actual false assertion.
